# Preface {.unnumbered}

Version: {{< meta version >}}

Welcome to *Data Science in Engineering*, a master's course at Trier University of Applied Sciences for students of mechanical engineering, electrical engineering and industrial engineering.

## What this course is about

Every method in this script is introduced together with a real, publicly available engineering dataset – from power plants and gas turbines to rolling bearings, semiconductor production and jet engines. Theory and practice go hand in hand: each chapter starts with a (fictional) engineering scenario that calls for a decision, explains the methods needed to make it, applies them in Python – and returns to the scenario at the end to make the decision with the results.

The course has four parts:

| Part | Topics | Chapters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A – Understanding Data | workflow, exploratory analysis, data quality, uncertainty | 1–3 |
| B – Statistics for Engineers | hypothesis tests, regression, design of experiments, model selection | 4–6 |
| C – Machine Learning | classification, ensembles, unsupervised learning, signal features | 7–10 |
| D – Time Series, Deep Learning and Review | forecasting, neural networks, review | 11–13 |

## Prerequisites

Basic Python programming and mathematics at bachelor level (linear algebra, calculus, introductory statistics).

## How to work with this script

The script is meant to be read in the browser or as a PDF. Every result in it was computed with Python, and the code is part of the script: in the HTML version, click *Code* above a result to show it. You can copy it into your own notebook to reproduce or vary an analysis.

During the semester, the demo code from the lectures is provided as Jupyter notebooks.

### Software

You can work with any development environment you like (e.g. JupyterLab, VS Code or PyCharm), as long as it can open, run and edit Jupyter notebooks. We recommend Google Colab; a local installation is an alternative:

- **Google Colab (recommended):** [Colab](https://colab.research.google.com) runs notebooks in the browser – no installation required, on a laptop or a tablet (an external keyboard helps a lot). Sign in with a Google account and open a notebook via *File → Upload notebook*. Most packages used in this course are pre-installed.
- **Alternative – local installation:** The [Anaconda Distribution](https://www.anaconda.com/download) installs Python, Jupyter and the most important data science packages in one go – a good choice if you prefer to work offline and with files on your own computer.

Packages that are missing can be installed directly from a notebook cell with `%pip install`, e.g. `%pip install ucimlrepo`.

### Reading guide

Each chapter opens with a scenario (purple box) and closes it in a section *Back to the decision*. The people and situations are invented; the data are real (or, where stated, simulated).

Coloured boxes highlight what matters most:

::: {.callout-note}
## Definitions
Blue boxes define the central concepts.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Key results
Red boxes contain theorems, key results and the takeaways at the end of each chapter.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfalls
Yellow boxes warn of typical mistakes – in data science, many of them lead to results that look convincing but are wrong.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Engineering practice
Green boxes give practical advice for engineering projects.
:::

Each chapter ends with exercises (highlighted boxes) followed by **solutions**, which are collapsed in the HTML version – try the exercise first, then open the solution. The lab assignments of the course build on the exercises.

Sections and exercises marked **Extension** go beyond the core of the course. They are optional and not required for the exam – use them to dig deeper into topics that matter for your own work.

### Notation

The script uses the following conventions throughout:

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| $x_1, \dots, x_n$ | observations (sample of size $n$); $x_i$ is the $i$-th observation |
| $\bar x$, $s$ | sample mean and sample standard deviation |
| $\tilde x$ | sample median |
| $\mu$, $\sigma$ | mean and standard deviation of the population or distribution |
| $\hat\theta$ | estimate of a parameter $\theta$ (the hat marks anything computed from data) |
| $y$, $\hat y$ | response (target) and its prediction |
| $X$ | matrix of inputs: one row per observation, one column per input |
| $P(A)$, $P(A \mid B)$ | probability, conditional probability |
| $E[X]$, $\text{Var}(X)$ | expected value and variance of a random variable $X$ |
| $\ln$ | natural logarithm |

The Greek alphabet is small, and the standard symbols of different fields overlap. Where a symbol has different meanings in different chapters, the meaning is stated where it is used. The most important cases: $\beta$ is the Weibull shape parameter (Chapter 3), the probability of a type II error (Chapter 4) and a regression coefficient (Chapters 5–7); $\eta$ is the Weibull scale parameter (Chapter 3) and the learning rate (Chapter 12); $\sigma$ denotes a standard deviation and, in Chapters 7 and 12, an activation function.

## Assessment

- **Lab assignments** (coursework, pass/fail): four assignments during the semester.
- **Written exam** (90 minutes, without computer): method choice, interpretation of results, short calculations and code reading.

Both parts must be passed; they can be completed in different semesters.
